newsitem.title: GERMANY: German guerrilla freed after six years in jail.
newsitem.headline: German guerrilla freed after six years in jail.

text.p: A former German leftist guerrilla convicted of shooting a Paris police officer 26 years ago was released from jail after spending six years of her 13-year sentence in jail, a German court said on Friday.

Inge Viett, the last of former Red Army Faction (RAF) guerrillas to be jailed after she was discovered hiding in East Germany in 1990, was also implicated in a 1979 attack on then-NATO commander Alexander Haig.

Viett was sentenced to 13 years in jail by a court in Koblenz in 1992 for shooting and permanently crippling a French police officer when he checked her identity papers in 1981. She was acquitted of helping prepare the attack on Haig.
"Viett has been released and put on parole," the Koblenz court said in a statement.

Viett, 53, was discovered living in East Germany on the eve of German unity in 1990 along with seven other retired RAF guerrillas who had been given cover in the former communist state from the late 1970s.
Prosecutors had demanded a life sentence for Viett, but the court rewarded her detailed testimony on former ties between the RAF and East Germany's Stasi security police.
Prosecutors had also charged her with supplying a machine pistol to RAF guerrillas who detonated a bomb near Haig's motorcade in Belgium. Haig was not injured.

Viett revealed close links with the Stasi, including training for RAF fighters at an East German camp for an unsuccessful 1981 grenade attack on U.S. General Frederick Kroessen in the West German town of Heidelberg.
Formed in the early 1970s as the Baader-Meinhoff gang, the group waged a war of assassinations and kidnappings against the establishment.
